title: U.S. House · Utah's 1st District
area: Northern Utah, drawn under the congressional map used for the first time in 2026 after a court struck down the Legislature's 2021 map; includes Ogden and Davis County.

context.text: This is an open seat. A Third District Court judge struck down Utah's 2021 congressional map in League of Women Voters v. Utah State Legislature and adopted a new map for 2026 that added a Democratic-leaning district. Under the new lines, incumbent Blake Moore (previously representing the old 1st District) is running in the new 2nd District, and incumbent Burgess Owens (previously representing the old 4th District, which included much of this area) is not seeking re-election, leaving this seat open. No candidate currently holds this specific redrawn district.

Ben McAdams, a former U.S. Representative (Utah's 4th District, 2019-2021) and former Salt Lake County Mayor, won the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary with 51.9% of the vote (29,737 of 57,295 votes, certified results per Ballotpedia) over Nate Blouin, Liban Mohamed and Michael Farrell. Riley Owen advanced from the Republican convention (the Republican primary was canceled after only one candidate qualified).

candidates.name: Ben McAdams
candidates.ballotNote: Won the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary with 51.9% of the vote (29,737 of 57,295 votes, certified results per Ballotpedia)

summary.text: Ben McAdams is the Democratic nominee for Utah's open 1st Congressional District. A Utah native and attorney, he served in the Utah State Senate, as Salt Lake County Mayor (2013-2019), and for one term as U.S. Representative for the 4th District (2019-2021), losing re-election in 2020. He won the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary and is running on affordability, opposition to Trump administration immigration enforcement tactics, and defending democratic institutions.

background.text: Born December 5, 1974, in West Bountiful, Utah.
Earned a bachelor's degree in political science from the University of Utah (2000) and a law degree from Columbia Law School (2003).

Began his legal career as an associate at Davis Polk & Wardwell in New York, then returned to Utah and practiced securities law at Dorsey & Whitney in Salt Lake City, according to Wikipedia. He later served as an adjunct professor at the University of Utah School of Law.
Worked as a senior advisor to Salt Lake City Mayor Ralph Becker, per Wikipedia; his campaign website cites that role and his work on a Salt Lake City LGBT non-discrimination ordinance.
Represented District 2 in the Utah State Senate after winning a special election to replace Scott McCoy, serving until he was elected Salt Lake County Mayor in 2012.
Served as Salt Lake County Mayor from January 2013 to January 2019, winning re-election in 2016.

Elected in 2018 to Utah's 4th Congressional District, defeating Republican incumbent Mia Love, and served 2019-2021 on the Committee on Financial Services and the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology. He lost re-election in 2020 to Burgess Owens by a margin of under 1%, per Wikipedia.

After leaving Congress, worked as CEO of Propvizer and the Common Ground Institute, and as a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and Sorenson Impact; he has also been affiliated with Utah's Promise and the Site Readiness for Good Jobs Fund.

Announced his candidacy for the redrawn 1st District in November 2025 after a court ordered Utah's congressional map redrawn. He lost the April 25 Democratic convention to Liban Mohamed (51.5% to 48.5% on the final ballot) but gathered signatures and won the June 23, 2026 primary with 51.9% over Nate Blouin, Liban Mohamed, and Michael Farrell.

priorities.text: Lowering costs for working families: opposes tariffs he says are driving up grocery and everyday prices, wants to expand affordable housing supply, and lower health care costs.
Says he will oppose what he describes as ICE's "lawless and dangerous raids" and work to "dismantle the current enforcement model that relies on fear and indiscriminate raids."
priorities.quote: ICE is broken; operating without accountability and oversight. ICE violence and unlawfulness must stop.

priorities.text: Defending democracy and the rule of law, including opposing what he calls the weaponization of the Justice Department, and protecting public lands including the Great Salt Lake.

positions.summary: Says decisions about abortion should be made by a woman, her doctor and the people she trusts, not politicians, and supports codifying Roe v. Wade into federal law.
positions.quote: Decisions about abortion should be made by a woman, her doctor, and the people she trusts, not politicians.

positions.summary: Opposes current ICE enforcement practices, calling for a system "rooted in constitutional protections," and supports a pathway to citizenship for Dreamers and other immigrants.
Says he opposes tariffs he attributes to the Trump administration, arguing they raise grocery and everyday costs for Utah families.
Calls climate change "an existential threat" and supports expanding clean energy and modernizing the electrical grid.
Says he will work to increase housing supply and cut red tape that drives up housing costs.

record.text: As a U.S. Representative (116th Congress), voted to impeach President Trump on both articles of impeachment in December 2019.
Voted for the Equality Act (H.R. 5), which would ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; passed the House 236-173.
Voted for the Great American Outdoors Act, which permanently funds the Land and Water Conservation Fund.
As Salt Lake County Mayor, created the Office for New Americans and launched the United for Citizenship Initiative to help permanent residents become U.S. citizens.

candidates.name: Riley Owen
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the April 25, 2026 Republican convention (primary was canceled)

summary.text: Riley Owen is the Republican nominee for Utah's open 1st Congressional District. A Salt Lake City resident in his twenties, he is a U.S. Navy Reserve intelligence officer and says he was a White House political appointee on trade and manufacturing policy before working in the shipbuilding, critical minerals and drone industries. He won the nomination at the April 2026 Republican convention and says he is running to defend children and families and to stop career politicians.

background.text: Says he comes from six generations of Utahns; he lives in Salt Lake City and was 27 when he announced his campaign, according to KSL.
Studied international relations at Princeton University, graduating with High Honors, and was an Eisenhower Scholar at Oxford University, earning a Master of Public Policy with Merit.
Served as a White House political appointee working on trade and manufacturing policy; KUER describes him as a former Trump White House staffer.
After government service, worked in industry in shipbuilding, critical minerals and drones; Ballotpedia also lists CEO among his career experience.
Serves as an intelligence officer in the U.S. Navy Reserve.
Won the Republican nomination outright with 71.2% of the delegate vote at the April 25, 2026 Utah Republican convention, so no Republican primary was held.
Told KUER he is focusing on affordability, business tax credits for paid maternity leave, and housing.

priorities.text: "Defend our kids. Support our families. Stop career politicians." — his stated three key campaign messages.
priorities.quote: Defend our kids. Support our families. Stop career politicians.

priorities.text: Says he is personally passionate about foreign affairs, national security, conservation and industrial policy.
Says he supports congressional term limits and a ban on stock trading by members of Congress, staffers and federal officials, and opposes the Citizens United decision.
priorities.quote: I support term limits for Congress. I support bans on stock trading for members, staffers and federal officials.

positions.summary: Calls for supply-side housing policy, including zoning reform that allows multi-family homes and accessory dwelling units.
positions.quote: Let’s solve this with supply-side solutions like common sense zoning reform enabling multi-family homes and accessory dwelling units.

candidates.researchNotes: Owen has not held prior elected office; no record items available. His campaign site (utahriley.com) could not be loaded (bot-check page), so his site text is taken from Ballotpedia's verbatim quote of it. Added a stated priority from the Salt Lake Tribune candidate questionnaire (Oct. 12, 2026); no further statements matched the guide's issue list.

candidates.name: Jesse West
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the April 18, 2026 Libertarian Party convention

summary.text: Jesse West is the Libertarian Party nominee for Utah's open 1st Congressional District. He is an attorney who has worked at several law firms and has also owned a hemp farm. He advanced from the Libertarian convention on April 18, 2026; he has not completed Ballotpedia's 2026 Candidate Connection survey.

background.text: Graduated from Cleveland High School in 2013, then earned a bachelor's degree in history from the University of Tennessee, Knoxville (2017) and a law degree from Lincoln Memorial University (2021).

Has worked as an attorney, including as an associate attorney at Jess Couser Family Law, Cowdin and Gatewood, and Long Okura, P.C., and has also worked as an executive coordinator, law clerk, and contract administrator.
Has owned Husky Hemp Farm and has been affiliated with the Utah Libertarian Party, the Tennessee Growers Coalition, and the Mushroom Society of Utah.
Advanced from the Libertarian Party convention for the 1st District on April 18, 2026.

priorities.text: Foreign policy: says troops should be brought home and defense should mean defending rather than nation-building.
priorities.quote: The best way to support the troops is to bring them home.

priorities.text: Criminal justice: proposes abolishing the federal death penalty.
priorities.quote: Abolish the death penalty at the federal level

priorities.text: Immigration: proposes clear pathways to citizenship and integration.
priorities.quote: Create clear, straightforward pathways to citizenship and integration.

positions.summary: Lists requiring congressional authorization for any new military engagement among his specific proposals.
positions.quote: Require Congressional authorization for any new military engagement

positions.summary: Calls for abolishing ICE, reducing DHS and cutting spending on detention, walls and deportation.
positions.quote: ICE must go and the DHS needs to be reduced significantly.

positions.summary: Lists repealing zoning laws that restrict housing supply among his economic proposals.
positions.quote: Repeal zoning laws that restrict home businesses and housing supply

candidates.researchNotes: Positions and statements come from West's campaign platform page (jessewest2026.com/policy) and his answers to the Salt Lake Tribune candidate questionnaire (Oct. 12, 2026). He did not complete a Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey. No stated positions found on abortion, guns, minimum wage, tariffs or voter citizenship proof.

statements.quote: The fix isn't more government. It's less.
Simplify the tax code and lower rates across the board
End taxpayer subsidies for fossil fuel extraction on public lands
I would work to cut funding to Israel
statements.context: In the Salt Lake Tribune candidate questionnaire, Oct. 12, 2026

candidates.name: Elias Montgomery

summary.text: Elias Montgomery is an unaffiliated candidate for Utah's open 1st Congressional District and a recent University of Utah graduate who works as a policy analyst. He describes himself as an independent alternative to the two major parties, focused on housing costs and what he calls a "broken political system." His platform includes limits on institutional purchases of single-family homes, "missing-middle" housing, and a proportional nomination model for parties.

background.text: Graduated from West Jordan High School and earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Utah in 2025.
Works as a policy analyst.

Runs as an unaffiliated candidate; in his Ballotpedia survey he lists key messages on housing affordability, restoring voter power through a proportional nomination model and ending corporate subsidies, and local control, including opposition to the Box Elder data center proposal.

priorities.text: Housing affordability: wants to discourage large-scale institutional purchase of single-family homes and legalize "missing-middle" housing like duplexes and townhomes.

Government-process reform: proposes a "proportional nomination model" requiring parties to nominate candidates in proportion to voter affiliation, a ban on omnibus spending bills, and a public real-time ledger for federal transactions.

Local control: says decisions on zoning and development should stay with local communities, and opposes fast-tracking large industrial projects like a proposed Box Elder County data center without standard public hearings.

positions.summary: Supports streamlining approval of "missing-middle" housing such as duplexes and townhomes while limiting large-scale corporate purchases of single-family homes.
positions.quote: Legalize and streamline "missing-middle" housing like duplexes, townhomes, and small apartments.

statements.quote: Criminalizing abortion does not work to eradicate the practice.

Shift law enforcement focus away from penalizing lawful gun owners and redirect resources to aggressively tracking and prosecuting violent felons, straw-purchasers, and criminal syndicates running black-market weapon networks.
statements.context: On his campaign website (Gun Rights plank)

statements.quote: Redirect enforcement assets entirely to high-impact tracking models targeting violent transnational syndicates and cartels.
statements.context: On his campaign website (Immigration Enforcement plank)

statements.quote: Provide robust community funding for advanced law enforcement training, mental health resources, and competitive retention pay.
statements.context: On his campaign website (Police Reform plank)

statements.quote: Pass a universal catastrophic healthcare floor to shield every family from medical bankruptcy.
Empower communities to develop advanced small-scale nuclear and solar setups without waiting through multi-year federal administrative freezes.
statements.context: On his campaign website (Climate Policy plank)

candidates.researchNotes: Statements come from the issue planks on Montgomery's campaign website (eliasmontgomery.com) and his Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey. He did not answer the Salt Lake Tribune candidate questionnaire. His planks do not take a direct side on the guide's issue statements, so no stances are recorded.

researchNotes: Utah's congressional map was redrawn by court order for 2026; this seat has no incumbent under the new lines. Riley Owen and Jesse West have limited public policy statements beyond Ballotpedia, and Jesse West has not completed Ballotpedia's 2026 Candidate Connection survey, so his biography rests on a brief Ballotpedia profile. Write-in candidate Bobby Darvish was omitted for lack of any documented public record. Sources differ on the year Ben McAdams entered the Utah State Senate, so the start year is omitted.
